title: Density
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The density (more precisely, the volumetric mass density; also known as specific mass), of a substance is its mass per unit volume. The symbol most often used for density is Ï (the lower case Greek letter rho), although the Latin letter D can also be used. Mathematically, density is defined as mass divided by volume

title: Standard Atomic Weight
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The standard atomic weight (Ar, standard) of a chemical element is the weighted arithmetic mean of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of all isotopes of that element weighted by each isotope's abundance on Earth. The standard atomic weight of each chemical element is determined and published by the Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW) of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) based on natural, stable, terrestrial sources of the element. It is the most common and practical atomic weight used by scientists.

title: Atomic Radius
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The atomic radius of a chemical element is a measure of the size of its atoms, usually the mean or typical distance from the center of the nucleus to the boundary of the surrounding shells of electrons. Since the boundary is not a well-defined physical entity, there are various non-equivalent definitions of atomic radius. Three widely used definitions of atomic radius are: Van der Waals radius, ionic radius, and covalent radius.

title: Electronegativity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Electronegativity, symbol Ï, is a concept that describes the tendency of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons (or electron density) towards itself. An atom's electronegativity is affected by both its atomic number and the distance at which its valence electrons reside from the charged nucleus. The higher the associated electronegativity number, the more an atom or a substituent group attracts electrons towards itself.

title: Ionization energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics, reactions. In physics and chemistry, ionization energy (American English spelling) or ionisation energy (British English spelling), denoted Ei, is the minimum amount of energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron, the valence electron, of an isolated neutral gaseous atom or molecule.

title: Electron configuration
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. In atomic physics and quantum chemistry, the electron configuration is the distribution of electrons of an atom or molecule (or other physical structure) in atomic or molecular orbitals

title: Enthalpy of fusion
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The enthalpy of fusion of a substance, also known as (latent) heat of fusion is the change in its enthalpy resulting from providing energy, typically heat, to a specific quantity of the substance to change its state from a solid to a liquid, at constant pressure.

title: Specific heat capacity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat capacity of a sample of the substance divided by the mass of the sample. Informally, it is the amount of energy that must be added, in the form of heat, to one unit of mass of the substance in order to cause an increase of one unit in its temperature.

title: Enthalpy of vaporization
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The enthalpy of vaporization, (symbol âHvap) also known as the (latent) heat of vaporization or heat of evaporation, is the amount of energy (enthalpy) that must be added to a liquid substance, to transform a quantity of that substance into a gas. The enthalpy of vaporization is a function of the pressure at which that transformation takes place.

title: Solubility chart
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. A solubility chart is a chart with a list of ions and how, when mixed with other ions, they can become precipitates or remain aqueous.

title: Superconductivity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Superconductivity is the set of physical properties observed in certain materials where electrical resistance vanishes and magnetic flux fields are expelled from the material. Any material exhibiting these properties is a superconductor.

title: Electrical resistivity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Electrical resistivity (also called specific electrical resistance or volume resistivity) and its inverse, electrical conductivity, is a fundamental property of a material that quantifies how strongly it resists or conducts electric current.

title: Electrical conductivity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Electrical conductivity or specific conductance is the reciprocal of electrical resistivity. It represents a material's ability to conduct electric current.

title: Thermodynamic temperature
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Thermodynamic temperature is the absolute measure of temperature and is one of the principal parameters of thermodynamics

title: Absolute zero
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Absolute zero is the lowest limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale, a state at which the enthalpy and entropy of a cooled ideal gas reach their minimum value, taken as zero kelvins.

title: Acid
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. An acid is a molecule or ion capable of donating a proton (hydrogen ion H+) (a BrÃ¸nstedâLowry acid), or, alternatively, capable of forming a covalent bond with an electron pair (a Lewis acid).

title: Activation energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. In chemistry and physics, activation energy is the energy which must be provided to a chemical or nuclear system with potential reactants to result in: a chemical reaction, nuclear reaction, or various other physical phenomena.

title: Chemical element
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. In chemistry, an element is a pure substance which cannot be broken down by chemical means, consisting of atoms which have identical numbers of protons in their atomic nuclei. The number of protons in the nucleus is the defining property of an element, and is referred to as the atomic number (represented by the symbol Z). Chemical elements constitute all of the baryonic matter of the universe.

title: Electron
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The electron is a subatomic particle whose electric charge is negative one elementary charge.

title: Proton
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. A proton is a subatomic particle with a positive electric charge of +1e elementary charge and a mass slightly less than that of a neutron.

title: Neutron
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The neutron is a subatomic particle with no electric charge and a mass slightly greater than that of a proton

title: Block (periodic table)
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A block of the periodic table is a set of elements unified by the orbitals their valence electrons or vacancies lie in.

title: Period (periodic table)
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A period in the periodic table is a row of chemical elements

title: Covalent radius
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The covalent radius is a measure of the size of an atom that forms part of one covalent bond.

title: Van der Waals radius
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The van der Waals radius of an atom is the radius of an imaginary hard sphere representing the distance of closest approach for another atom.

title: Dark Matter
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Dark matter is a form of matter thought to account for approximately 85% of the matter in the universe and about a quarter of its total massâenergy density or about 2.241Ã10^â27 kg/m3.

title: Elementary Particle
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In physics, an elementary particle or fundamental particle is a particle that is not made of other particles.

title: Fats
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. In nutrition, biology, and chemistry, fat usually means any ester of fatty acids, or a mixture of such compounds; most commonly those that occur in living beings or in food.

title: Functional Group
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. In organic chemistry, functional groups are specific substituents or moieties within molecules that may be responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of those molecules.

title: Hydrophile
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A hydrophile is a molecule or other molecular entity that is attracted to water molecules and tends to be dissolved by water.

title: Hydrophobe
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. In chemistry, hydrophobicity is the physical property of a molecule that is seemingly repelled from a mass of water (known as a hydrophobe).

title: Isotope
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Isotopes are variants of a particular chemical element which differ in neutron number, and consequently in nucleon number.

title: Liquid
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A liquid is a nearly incompressible fluid that conforms to the shape of its container but retains a (nearly) constant volume independent of pressure.

title: Macromolecule
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A macromolecule is a very large molecule, such as protein, commonly composed of the polymerization of smaller subunits called monomers. They are typically composed of thousands of atoms or more.

title: Magnetic Field
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A magnetic field is a vector field (more precisely a pseudovector field) that describes the magnetic influence of electric charges in relative motion and magnetized materials.

title: Gas
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Gas is one of the four fundamental states of matter (the others being solid, liquid, and plasma). A pure gas may be made up of individual atoms (e.g. a noble gas like neon), elemental molecules made from one type of atom (e.g. oxygen), or compound molecules made from a variety of atoms (e.g. carbon dioxide).

title: Molar Mass
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. In chemistry, the molar mass is defined as the mass of a sample of that compound divided by the amount of substance in that sample, measured in moles.

title: Nuclear Matter
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Nuclear matter is an idealized system of interacting nucleons (protons and neutrons) that exists in several phases that as yet are not fully established.

title: Pressure
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Pressure (symbol: p or P) is the force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit area over which that force is distributed.

title: Rust
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Rust is an iron oxide, a usually reddish brown oxide formed by the reaction of iron and oxygen in the presence of water or air moisture.

title: Semiconductors
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A semiconductor material has an electrical conductivity value falling between that of a conductor, such as metallic copper, and an insulator, such as glass.

title: Solubility
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Solubility is the property of a solid, liquid or gaseous chemical substance called solute to dissolve in a solid, liquid or gaseous solvent.

title: Spectrometer
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A spectrometer (/spÉkËtrÉmÉªtÉr/) is a scientific instrument used to separate and measure spectral components of a physical phenomenon.

title: Vacuum
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Vacuum is space devoid of matter. The word stems from the Latin adjective vacuus for "vacant" or "void". An approximation to such vacuum is a region with a gaseous pressure much less than atmospheric pressure.

title: Wavelength
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics,math. In physics, the wavelength is the spatial period of a periodic waveâthe distance over which the wave's shape repeats. It is the distance between consecutive corresponding points of the same phase on the wave, such as two adjacent crests, troughs, or zero crossings, and is a characteristic of both traveling waves and standing waves, as well as other spatial wave patterns.

title: Weight
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. In science and engineering, the weight of an object is the force acting on the object due to gravity.

title: White Noise
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In signal processing, white noise is a random signal having equal intensity at different frequencies, giving it a constant power spectral density.

title: Frequency
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics, math. Frequency is the number of occurrences of a repeating event per unit of time.

title: Friction
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Friction is the force resisting the relative motion of solid surfaces, fluid layers, and material elements sliding against each other.

title: Efficiency
text: Dictionary entry in categories math. Efficiency is the amount of divisions ordered from a task. In more mathematical or scientific terms, it is a measure of the extent to which input is well used for an intended task or function (output).

title: Impulse
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In classical mechanics, impulse (symbolized by J or Imp) is the integral of a force, F, over the time interval, t, for which it acts. Since force is a vector quantity, impulse is also a vector quantity.

title: Intensity
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In physics, intensity of radiant energy is the power transferred per unit area, where the area is measured on the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the energy.

title: Centripetal Force
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A centripetal force (from Latin centrum, "center" and petere, "to seek") is a force that makes a body follow a curved path. Its direction is always orthogonal to the motion of the body and towards the fixed point of the instantaneous center of curvature of the path.

title: Momentum
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In Newtonian mechanics, linear momentum, translational momentum, or simply momentum (pl. momenta) is the product of the mass and velocity of an object.

title: Spectrum
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A spectrum (plural spectra or spectrums) is a condition that is not limited to a specific set of values but can vary, without steps, across a continuum. The word was first used scientifically in optics to describe the rainbow of colors in visible light after passing through a prism. As scientific understanding of light advanced, it came to apply to the entire electromagnetic spectrum. It thereby became a mapping of a range of magnitudes (wavelengths) to a range of qualities, which are the perceived "colors of the rainbow" and other properties which correspond to wavelengths that lie outside of the visible light spectrum.

title: Electromagnetic Spectrum
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The electromagnetic spectrum is the range of frequencies (the spectrum) of electromagnetic radiation and their respective wavelengths and photon energies.

title: Electric Charge
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Electric charge is the physical property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field. There are two types of electric charge: positive and negative (commonly carried by protons and electrons respectively). Like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract each other. An object with an absence of net charge is referred to as neutral.

title: Matter
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. In classical physics and general chemistry, matter is any substance that has mass and takes up space by having volume. All everyday objects that can be touched are ultimately composed of atoms, which are made up of interacting subatomic particles, and in everyday as well as scientific usage, "matter" generally includes atoms and anything made up of them, and any particles (or combination of particles) that act as if they have both rest mass and volume

title: Photon
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The photon (Greek: Ïá¿¶Ï, phÅs, light) is a type of elementary particle. It is the quantum of the electromagnetic field including electromagnetic radiation such as light and radio waves, and the force carrier for the electromagnetic force. Photons are massless, so they always move at the speed of light in vacuum, 299792458 m/s (or about 186,282 mi/s). The photon belongs to the class of bosons.

title: Boson
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In quantum mechanics, a boson is a particle that follows BoseâEinstein statistics. Bosons make up one of two classes of elementary particles, the other being fermions. The name boson was coined by Paul Dirac to commemorate the contribution of Satyendra Nath Bose, an Indian physicist and professor of physics at University of Calcutta and at University of Dhaka in developing, with Albert Einstein, BoseâEinstein statistics, which theorizes the characteristics of elementary particles.

title: Fermion
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In particle physics, a fermion is a particle that follows FermiâDirac statistics and generally has half odd integer spin: spin 1/2, spin 3/2, etc. These particles obey the Pauli exclusion principle. Fermions include all quarks and leptons, as well as all composite particles made of an odd number of these, such as all baryons and many atoms and nuclei. Fermions differ from bosons, which obey BoseâEinstein statistics.

title: Quark
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A quark is a type of elementary particle and a fundamental constituent of matter. Quarks combine to form composite particles called hadrons, the most stable of which are protons and neutrons, the components of atomic nuclei. All commonly observable matter is composed of up quarks, down quarks and electrons.

title: Lepton
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In particle physics, a lepton is an elementary particle of half-integer spin (spin 1â2) that does not undergo strong interactions. Two main classes of leptons exist: charged leptons (also known as the electron-like leptons or muons), and neutral leptons (better known as neutrinos). Charged leptons can combine with other particles to form various composite particles such as atoms and positronium, while neutrinos rarely interact with anything, and are consequently rarely observed. The best known of all leptons is the electron.

title: Particle Accelerator
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. A particle accelerator is a machine that uses electromagnetic fields to propel charged particles to very high speeds and energies, and to contain them in well-defined beams.

title: Electric Field
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. An electric field (sometimes E-field) is the physical field that surrounds electrically-charged particles and exerts force on all other charged particles in the field, either attracting or repelling them. It also refers to the physical field for a system of charged particles. Electric fields originate from electric charges, or from time-varying magnetic fields. Electric fields and magnetic fields are both manifestations of the electromagnetic force, one of the four fundamental forces (or interactions) of nature.

title: Molecule
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds. Molecules are distinguished from ions by their lack of electrical charge.

title: Hydrogen Bond
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. A hydrogen bond (often informally abbreviated H-bond) is a primarily electrostatic force of attraction between a hydrogen (H) atom which is covalently bound to a more electronegative atom or group, and another electronegative atom bearing a lone pair of electronsâthe hydrogen bond acceptor (Ac). Such an interacting system is generally denoted DnâHÂ·Â·Â·Ac, where the solid line denotes a polar covalent bond, and the dotted or dashed line indicates the hydrogen bond

title: Van Der Waals Force
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. In molecular physics, the Van der Waals force, named after Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals, is a distance-dependent interaction between atoms or molecules. Unlike ionic or covalent bonds, these attractions do not result from a chemical electronic bond; they are comparatively weak and therefore more susceptible to disturbance. The Van der Waals force quickly vanishes at longer distances between interacting molecules.

title: Ionic Bonding
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. Ionic bonding is a type of chemical bonding that involves the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, or between two atoms with sharply different electronegativities, and is the primary interaction occurring in ionic compounds.

title: Ion
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. An ion is a particle, atom or molecule with a net electrical charge.

title: Cation
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. A cation is an ion with fewer electrons than protons, giving it a positive charge.

title: Anion
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. An anion is an ion with more electrons than protons, giving it a net negative charge (since electrons are negatively charged and protons are positively charged).

title: Energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In physics, energy is the quantitative property that must be transferred to a body or physical system to perform work on the object, or to heat it. Energy is a conserved quantity; the law of conservation of energy states that energy can be converted in form, but not created or destroyed. The unit of measurement in the International System of Units (SI) of energy is the joule, which is the energy transferred to an object by the work of moving it a distance of one metre against a force of one newton.

title: Elastic Energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Elastic energy is the mechanical potential energy stored in the configuration of a material or physical system as it is subjected to elastic deformation by work performed upon it. Elastic energy occurs when objects are impermanently compressed, stretched or generally deformed in any manner

title: Kinetic Energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In physics, the kinetic energy of an object is the energy that it possesses due to its motion. It is defined as the work needed to accelerate a body of a given mass from rest to its stated velocity. Having gained this energy during its acceleration, the body maintains this kinetic energy unless its speed changes. The same amount of work is done by the body when decelerating from its current speed to a state of rest.

title: Potential Energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. In physics, potential energy is the energy held by an object because of its position relative to other objects, stresses within itself, its electric charge, or other factors.

title: Mass
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics, chemistry. Mass is both a property of a physical body and a measure of its resistance to acceleration (rate of change of velocity with respect to time) when a net force is applied. An object's mass also determines the strength of its gravitational attraction to other bodies.

title: Measure
text: Dictionary entry in categories math. In mathematics, a measure on a set is a systematic way to assign a number, intuitively interpreted as its size, to some subsets of that set, called measurable sets. In this sense, a measure is a generalization of the concepts of length, area, and volume. A particularly important example is the Lebesgue measure on a Euclidean space, which assigns the usual length, area, or volume to subsets of a Euclidean spaces, for which this be defined. For instance, the Lebesgue measure of an interval of real numbers is its usual length.

title: Function
text: Dictionary entry in categories math. In mathematics, a function is a binary relation between two sets that associates to each element of the first set exactly one element of the second set. Typical examples are functions from integers to integers, or from the real numbers to real numbers.

title: Differentiable function
text: Dictionary entry in categories math. In calculus (a branch of mathematics), a differentiable function of one real variable is a function whose derivative exists at each point in its domain. In other words, the graph of a differentiable function has a non-vertical tangent line at each interior point in its domain. A differentiable function is smooth (the function is locally well approximated as a linear function at each interior point) and does not contain any break, angle, or cusp.

title: Calculus
text: Dictionary entry in categories math. Calculus, originally called infinitesimal calculus or "the calculus of infinitesimals", is the mathematical study of continuous change, in the same way that geometry is the study of shape and algebra is the study of generalizations of arithmetic operations.

title: Solid-Water Distribution Coefficient
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. To assess the extent to which a compound is associated with solid phases in a given system at equilibrium (see below), we need to know the ratio of the compound s total equilibrium concentrations in the solids and in the aqueous solution.

title: Avogadro constant
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The Avogadro constant (NA) is the number of constituent particles, usually atoms or molecules, contained in one mole of a substance. Its fixed value in SI units is approximately 6.02214076Ã10^23 mol^â1.

title: Planck constant
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The Planck constant (h) is a fundamental physical constant that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency via E = hÎ½. It is central to quantum mechanics.

title: Boltzmann constant
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The Boltzmann constant (k or kB) relates the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature; it appears in statistical mechanics and thermodynamics.

title: Ideal gas law
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas: PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, R is the gas constant, and T is temperature.

title: Entropy
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Entropy is a thermodynamic state function that measures the number of microscopic configurations corresponding to a macroscopic state; often interpreted as a measure of disorder or information.

title: Gibbs free energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The Gibbs free energy (G) is a thermodynamic potential that can be used to calculate the maximum reversible work that may be performed by a thermodynamic system at constant temperature and pressure. ÎG < 0 indicates a spontaneous process.

title: pH
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. pH is a logarithmic measure of the hydrogen ion concentration [H+] in an aqueous solution: pH = -log10[H+]. It indicates acidity (pH < 7) or basicity (pH > 7).

title: Equilibrium constant
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The equilibrium constant (K) of a chemical reaction is the ratio of the activities (often approximated by concentrations) of products to reactants at equilibrium, raised to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients.

title: Catalyst
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself being consumed; it provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

title: Reaction rate
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, reactions. Reaction rate is the change in concentration of reactants or products per unit time. It is influenced by temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts, and reaction mechanism.

title: Arrhenius equation
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The Arrhenius equation gives the temperature dependence of reaction rates: k = AÂ·e^(âEa/(RT)), where k is rate constant, A is frequency factor, Ea is activation energy, R is gas constant, and T is temperature.

title: Half-life (radioactive decay)
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. The half-life is the time required for half of a sample of a radioactive isotope to decay. For first-order decay, activity follows exponential decay and half-life is constant.

title: Fermi energy
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The Fermi energy is the energy of the highest occupied quantum state in a system of fermions at absolute zero temperature; it characterizes the electronic properties of metals and semiconductors.

title: Redox reaction
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A redox (reductionâoxidation) reaction involves the transfer of electrons between chemical species; oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.

title: Stoichiometry
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Stoichiometry is the calculation of reactants and products in chemical reactions, based on conservation of mass and atom counts determined by balanced chemical equations.

title: Mole (amount of substance)
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The mole is the SI unit for the amount of substance; one mole contains exactly Avogadro's number of specified entities (atoms, molecules, etc.).

title: Thermodynamic equilibrium
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Thermodynamic equilibrium is the state in which a system's macroscopic properties do not change in time and no net flows of matter or energy occur between subsystems.

title: First law of thermodynamics
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The first law states that energy is conserved: the change in internal energy of a system equals heat added to the system minus work done by the system.

title: Second law of thermodynamics
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The second law asserts that the total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease over time; processes tend toward increasing entropy and irreversibility.

title: Solvent
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A solvent is the component of a solution that is present in the greatest amount and dissolves a solute, forming a solution; water is the most common solvent in chemistry.

title: Solvation
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Solvation is the process of surrounding solute particles with solvent molecules; in water this process is called hydration.

title: Oxidation
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Oxidation is the loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation state by a molecule, atom, or ion during a chemical reaction.

title: Reduction
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Reduction is the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation state by a molecule, atom, or ion during a chemical reaction.

title: Buffer solution
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. A buffer solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, typically consisting of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or vice versa).

title: Compressibility
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Compressibility is a measure of the relative volume change of a fluid or solid as a response to a pressure change; isothermal compressibility and bulk modulus are related properties.

title: Viscosity
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to gradual deformation by shear stress or tensile stress; it describes internal friction in fluids.

title: Refractive index
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium, determining how much light is bent when entering the medium.

title: Dielectric constant
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. The dielectric constant (relative permittivity) is the ratio of the permittivity of a substance to the permittivity of free space, describing how an electric field affects and is affected by a medium.

title: Specific gravity
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance (usually water for liquids), a dimensionless quantity used to compare densities.

title: Surface tension
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Surface tension is the elastic tendency of a fluid surface which makes it acquire the least surface area possible, caused by cohesive forces between liquid molecules.

title: Phase diagram
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. A phase diagram is a graphical representation showing the equilibrium phases of a substance as a function of variables like temperature, pressure, and composition.

title: Latent heat
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released by a substance during a phase change (e.g., melting, vaporization) at constant temperature and pressure.

title: Partition coefficient
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The partition coefficient (P) is the ratio of concentrations of a compound in a two-phase system at equilibrium, commonly octanol/water, indicating hydrophobicity.

title: van 't Hoff factor
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The van 't Hoff factor (i) is the number of particles a compound yields in solution for colligative properties; it accounts for dissociation or association in solution.

title: Le Chatelier's principle
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Le Chatelier's principle states that if a dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing conditions (concentration, temperature, pressure), the system responds to counteract the change and re-establish equilibrium.

title: BornâHaber cycle
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. The BornâHaber cycle is a thermochemical series of steps that models the formation of an ionic solid from its constituent elements, used to calculate lattice energies.

title: Molarity
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Molarity (M) is a concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute per liter of solution.

title: Molality
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Molality (m) is a concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; it is temperature independent.

title: Partial pressure
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Partial pressure is the pressure that a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone occupied the entire volume; total pressure is the sum of partial pressures (Dalton's law).

title: Raoult's law
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Raoult's law states that the partial vapor pressure of each volatile component in an ideal solution equals the vapor pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction in the solution.

title: DebyeâHÃ¼ckel theory
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. DebyeâHÃ¼ckel theory describes the behavior of strong electrolytes in dilute solution by accounting for ionic atmosphere and electrostatic interactions, predicting activity coefficients.

title: Diffusion
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry, physics. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration due to random thermal motion; described by Fick's laws.

title: Brownian motion
text: Dictionary entry in categories physics. Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a fluid resulting from collisions with fast-moving molecules of the fluid; evidence of molecular kinetics.

title: Ionic strength
text: Dictionary entry in categories chemistry. Ionic strength is a measure of the total concentration of ions in solution, weighted by the square of their charges; it affects activity coefficients and reaction rates in electrolyte solutions.
